s: Part four.
Integrating M C P servers.
By the end of this part, you'll know where a server's wiring should live.
How secrets get in without being committed.
Which of three kinds of capability a feature belongs in.
And why a server's own labels are never permission.
The plain picture.
A house wired before standard sockets existed had every appliance connected by hand.
Moving the toaster meant calling an electrician.
So what makes a standard socket valuable?
The appliance and the building can be built by people who never meet.
M C P is that agreement, for the systems an agent reaches into.
Your ticket tracker.
Your document store.
Your internal services.
Wire a system up once behind the protocol, and anything that speaks it can reach it.
This task statement asks three narrower questions.
One.
Where do the wiring instructions live?
So the setup behaves the same on your laptop, and on a build server nobody is sitting at.
Two.
What names do the tools answer to, once connected?
Three.
Which kind of socket does a capability belong in?
The protocol offers three.
And they differ in who decides.
First.
Where the wiring lives.
Picture writing the team's shared phone list in your personal notebook.
It works perfectly for you.
And nobody else has it.
Now pin it on the office noticeboard, with each person's private PIN left for them to fill in.
Everyone gets the same list, without exposing anyone's details.
In Claude Code, M C P servers load at three scopes.
One.
Local scope.
It's the default for the claude mcp add command.
It's stored in the file at ~/.claude.json, under the current project's path.
And it's private to you.
Two.
Project scope.
It lives in a file called .mcp.json, at the repository root.
It's meant to be committed to version control, and shared.
Three.
User scope.
It also lives in ~/.claude.json, but applies across all of your projects.
And it's still private to you.
Question one.
Here's the scenario.
A developer connected a shared Postgres M C P server with claude mcp add, and no scope flag.
It works on their machine.
But two teammates who cloned the repository say the database tools aren't there.
The team wants everyone to get the same definition from version control.
Without anyone's password being committed.
Take a second.
The answer.
Define the server in a project-scoped .mcp.json at the repository root.
Reference the password as a variable, DB_PASSWORD, wrapped in the dollar-and-braces expansion syntax.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: re-add it with the user scope flag.
Why?
That widens the server across the developer's own projects.
But it still never reaches teammates.
Wrong: commit ~/.claude.json.
Why?
It leaks a personal file that can hold private entries, tokens, and other projects' settings.
Wrong: a README telling everyone to run the same command.
Why?
It relies on manual steps that drift.
The constraint phrase is "teammates lack the tools."
That almost always means move it to .mcp.json.
Now precedence.
The notes test this with a lovely trap.
When the same server name appears at more than one scope, Claude Code connects once.
It uses the highest-precedence definition.
And it takes that entry whole.
Fields are never merged.
The order has five steps.
Local.
Then project.
Then user.
Then servers bundled in plugins.
Then claude.ai connectors.
So picture this.
A team adds an Authorization header to the warehouse server, in the committed .mcp.json.
One developer added the same server months ago, with no scope flag.
That means local scope.
What happens?
Their session connects to their own stale local entry.
The header is simply absent.
And calls fail authentication.
The fix is to remove the local entry.
Not to edit the project file harder.
Wrong: copy the header into a private file.
Why?
That defeats the point of a shared definition.
Notice how this differs from CLAUDE.md files.
There, all scopes are additive, and the model reconciles contradictions by judgment.
We cover that contrast properly in the Claude Code configuration chapter.
Hold on to this line.
Shared servers go in .mcp.json, and the highest-precedence entry wins whole.
Second.
Secrets and variable expansion.
Picture a recipe card that says "add the house sauce from your own cupboard."
In a borrowed kitchen with no house sauce, a literal-minded cook pours in nothing but the label.
And the dish fails at the table, rather than in the kitchen.
The fix is to stock the borrowed kitchen.
Not to print the sauce on the card.
Claude Code expands two forms inside .mcp.json.
The plain form.
A dollar sign, and braces around a variable name.
It becomes that variable's value.
The form with a colon and hyphen after the name.
It becomes the variable if it's set, and a default otherwise.
Expansion works in five fields.
The command, args, env, url, and headers fields.
And the design rule?
Defaults on endpoints and paths, so a fresh clone works.
And no default, ever, on a secret.
So it must come from the developer's environment, or a secret store.
Question two.
Here's the scenario.
A committed .mcp.json passes an issue-tracker token as a bearer header, using ISSUE_TOKEN, with no default.
It works on every laptop.
In the continuous integration job, the server loads. claude mcp list prints a warning.
And every call fails authentication.
What's the cause, and what's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
ISSUE_TOKEN is unset in the build environment.
So the literal placeholder text is sent.
The fix is to inject the token from the pipeline's secret store.
This is a behaviour worth memorising.
An unset variable with no default does not fail loudly.
The configuration still loads.
The list command warns.
And the literal text is used.
That surfaces later as an authentication error, rather than a configuration error.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: claim the headers field does not expand variables, and add a second file with a hard-coded token.
Why?
The claim is factually wrong.
And the second file commits the secret.
Wrong: add a default containing a shared service token.
Why?
That commits a credential to version control.
Wrong: claim project servers need an approval the build cannot give, then disable the server.
Why?
It misses that the server is already loading.
And it removes the tracker, instead of fixing authentication.
The notes add a related case.
A committed file hard-codes a bearer token.
And staging engineers keep editing the URL locally, and accidentally committing it.
One change fixes both.
A variable with a production default, for the URL.
And a variable with no default, for the token.
Watch two distractors there.
Wrong: a bare dollar sign before the name, without braces.
Why?
That's not the supported syntax.
Wrong: put the token in a project .env file.
Why?
That doesn't take the secret out of the repository.
Three smaller traps in the same area.
One.
The variable CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR is set in the server's environment, not in Claude Code's own.
So a project-scoped file should give it a default of dot, meaning the current directory.
Two.
An HTTP server entry with a url but no type field is a configuration error.
Why?
Claude Code reads a typeless entry as a local stdio server, and skips it.
Three.
Project-scoped servers arrive through a git pull.
So Claude Code asks for interactive approval before using them.
A non-interactive run cannot show that prompt.
So if a server must stay out of automated runs, list it in disabledMcpjsonServers.
That blocks it in every mode.
The self-check pairs two of these.
They're the two likeliest reasons a committed .mcp.json works on laptops and fails in continuous integration.
A missing variable.
And an approval assumption.
Hold on to this line.
No default on secrets, defaults on endpoints, and an unset secret shows up later as an authentication failure.
Third.
The three kinds of capability.
Picture a fire alarm button that anyone can lean on.
So it goes off whenever someone brushes past.
A glass-fronted box, that you have to open on purpose, is still one step away.
But it only goes off when a person decides.
The fix is the housing.
Not a sign saying "please do not lean."
M C P servers expose three primitives.
And the difference is who is in control.
One.
Tools are model-controlled.
The model discovers them with tools/list, and invokes them with tools/call, on its own judgment.
Two.
Resources are application-driven.
The host application decides how to bring them in, through a picker, a search, or a mention.
It uses resources/list, resources/templates/list, and resources/read.
And each resource has a stable address, called a URI.
That's a uniform resource identifier.
Three.
Prompts are user-controlled.
A person selects them deliberately.
They're found with prompts/list, and fetched with prompts/get.
And in Claude Code, they appear as slash commands.
Question three.
Here's the scenario.
An internal server exposes run_release_checklist as a tool.
Release managers want to start it deliberately, at a moment they choose.
But the agent keeps invoking it whenever a conversation mentions a release.
And that pages the on-call team.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Expose it as an M C P prompt, so a person selects it.
For example, as a slash command.
The capability sits in the wrong primitive.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: keep it as a tool, with a sentence saying "call only when asked."
Why?
It leaves a model-controlled primitive in charge of a human decision.
Wrong: expose it as a resource.
Why?
That hands the decision to the host application.
Not to a person, at a moment they choose.
Wrong: set tool_choice to none on every request.
Why?
It disables every other tool too.
The other direction is just as tested.
The notes describe a server with nine thousand four hundred runbooks, behind a fetch_runbook tool that takes a title.
Agents fetch the wrong runbook, or three in a row.
The titles are stable, and organised by service and failure mode.
The fix?
Resources, with a resource template.
Its address pattern is runbook, colon, slash slash, then service, then failure mode.
Now the host can list, filter, and select by stable address.
And the model never guesses a name.
Resources also support subscribe and listChanged.
So a host learns when a document changes, instead of re-fetching.
Tools have no equivalent.
Now the wrong turns there.
Wrong: a longer description containing all the titles.
Why?
It floods the context.
Wrong: add a search tool.
Why?
It adds a hop, without removing the guesswork.
Wrong: prompts.
Why?
They're for deliberate human workflows, not a retrieval surface.
There's one case where a tool stays right.
Retrieval that needs model judgment, like ranked semantic search.
There, the model's phrasing of the query is the actual input.
The stem phrase to listen for is "the agent keeps fetching the wrong document."
That points to resources.
So.
Tool, resource, or prompt?
Ask who should decide.
If the model should reach for it on its own judgment, it's a tool.
If it's a catalog the application should present, it's a resource.
If a person must start it deliberately, it's a prompt.
Hold on to this line.
Match the primitive to who is in control.
Fourth.
The names things answer to.
Once connected, a server's tools are called mcp__, then the server name, then a double underscore, then the tool name.
That exact string goes in three places.
Permission rules.
A subagent's tools list.
And hook matchers.
Tools from a server bundled inside a plugin carry a longer prefix.
It includes the word plugin, and the plugin's name.
That's why a matcher written against the bare server key never fires for them.
Resources are referenced with an at sign, the server name, a colon, and the resource address.
Prompts are invoked as a slash, then mcp__, the server name, a double underscore, and the prompt name.
Fifth.
Annotations.
Picture a box labelled "fragile, books only" by the sender.
That tells you how to carry it.
Not what's inside.
If you need to be sure nothing risky leaves the building, you check at the door, and decide who may sign for it.
The label is the sender's word.
The door check is yours.
M C P lets a server annotate its tools with hints.
There are four, each with a default.
readOnlyHint defaults to false.
destructiveHint defaults to true.
idempotentHint defaults to false.
And openWorldHint defaults to true.
The specification requires clients to treat annotations as untrusted, unless they come from a trusted server.
As the M C P project's own blog puts it, a server can claim to be read-only, and still delete your files.
Question four.
This one is select two.
Here's the scenario.
A third-party server's export_repository tool declares readOnlyHint true.
But an export copies the entire repository to external storage.
The team requires a person to confirm every export.
And it wants only the release subagent able to export at all.
Which two measures have real enforcement?
Take a second.
The answers.
First, grant mcp__vendor__export_repository only in the release subagent's tools allowlist.
Second, write a permission rule against that exact tool name, requiring a person to approve each call.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: trust the hint, and skip confirmation.
Why?
That treats the server's self-description as authorization.
Wrong: a system prompt telling agents to ask first.
Why?
It's a request.
And it can be lost when the conversation is compacted.
Wrong: ask the vendor to switch to destructiveHint true.
Why?
That swaps one untrusted hint for another.
The notes have a matching story.
A host skipped confirmation because a dataset export tool claimed to be read-only.
And an agent triggered forty exports, and exhausted the storage budget.
The primary error was the host treating a hint as an authorization decision.
Two nuances.
First.
Advisory does not mean inert.
The Agent software development kit uses readOnlyHint when deciding whether a tool can run in parallel with other read-only tools.
So the hint can change scheduling.
That's how the agentic architecture chapter uses it.
But it never grants permission.
Second.
If a specific operation must always be confirmed, Claude Code honours a field in the tool's _meta called anthropic/requiresUserInteraction, set to true in its tools/list entry.
Hold on to this line.
Annotations are the sender's label.
Enforcement is your tool set and your permission rules.
Finally, one protocol change you should know exists.
The M C P specification dated the twenty-eighth of July, twenty twenty-six, replaced the stateful, session-based model with a stateless request-and-response protocol.
The plain version?
Picture a corner shop that used to keep a tab under your name.
Now it treats every purchase as standing on its own.
So any branch can serve you.
And a lost ledger costs nothing.
Technically, here's what changed.
The initialize handshake and the Mcp-Session-Id header are gone.
Requests are self-describing.
So any server instance behind a load balancer can take them.
Multi Round-Trip Requests carry mid-call questions, like confirmations, without a held-open connection.
Method and tool names travel in HTTP headers, so gateways can route without opening the body.
Tool, prompt and resource lists carry a time-to-live, and a cache hint.
Roots, Sampling, Logging, and the legacy HTTP plus Server-Sent Events transport are deprecated, with at least a twelve-month offramp.
And tools, resources and prompts are untouched.
So everything in this part still holds.
One exam caution.
The exam guide, version one point oh, effective July twenty twenty-six, predates this specification.
So an exam item may still assume the older session model.
Build against the new one in real work.
That's part four.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
Shared servers go in the committed project file, with secrets pulled from the environment.
And each capability goes in the primitive that matches who decides.
Coming up in part five: selecting and applying the built-in tools effectively.
